questions.question: A compressive force F acts on an object of Young modulus E, original length x and cross-sectional area A. Which expression gives the length after the force is applied? The options A to D are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: D: x - Fx / (AE)
steps: Stress = F / A and strain = stress / E = F / (AE).
The compression is strain x original length = Fx / (AE).
The force is compressive, so the length gets shorter: new length = x - Fx / (AE), which is option D.

questions.question: State what is meant by the elastic limit of a steel cable.
questions.answer: The maximum stress (or force) beyond which the material does not return to its original length when the load is removed, i.e. permanent deformation begins.
steps: Below the elastic limit the cable returns to its original length when the force is removed.
Beyond the elastic limit it is permanently deformed (plastic deformation).
So the elastic limit is the maximum stress up to which deformation is fully recoverable.

questions.question: A steel cable of length 6.00 m reaches its elastic limit at a force of 13.4 x 10^6 N and an extension of 0.126 m. Calculate the strain at the elastic limit.
questions.answer: Strain = 0.0210
steps: Strain = extension / original length.
Strain = 0.126 m / 6.00 m.
Strain = 0.0210 (no units).

questions.question: The steel cable has cross-sectional area 9.60 x 10^-3 m^2 and the force at its elastic limit is 13.4 x 10^6 N. Calculate the stress at the elastic limit.
questions.answer: Stress = 1.40 x 10^9 Pa
steps: Stress = force / cross-sectional area.
Stress = 1.40 x 10^9 Pa.

questions.question: A force is applied to a copper wire. Which row of the length and diameter table would give the greatest extension? The table is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: C: length 2x, diameter D
steps: Extension = F L / (A E), so for the same force and material extension is proportional to L / A, which is proportional to L / d^2.
Row A: x / D^2 = 1 unit, row B: x / (4D^2) = 0.25, row C: 2x / D^2 = 2, row D: 2x / (4D^2) = 0.5.
Row C has the largest value of L / d^2, so it gives the greatest extension.

questions.question: Which row of the table shows the correct application of the terms stiffness constant and Young modulus? The table is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: D: stiffness constant applies to objects, Young modulus applies to materials
steps: The stiffness constant k = F / x depends on the size and shape of the object (for a wire, k = EA / L).
The Young modulus is stress / strain, a property of the material that does not depend on the dimensions of the sample.
So the stiffness constant applies to objects and the Young modulus to materials: row D.

questions.question: A 50 cm wire extends by 2 mm under a load. Which option gives the strain? The options A to D are shown in the figure below.
steps: Strain = extension / original length.
Both in the same units: 2 mm / 500 mm = 0.004 (no units).

questions.question: A wire breaks under tensile force T. A second wire of the same material has twice the diameter. What force breaks the second wire? The options A to D are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: A: 4T
steps: The same material breaks at the same breaking stress, so the breaking force = breaking stress x area.
Area is proportional to d^2, so doubling the diameter gives 4 times the area.
The breaking force is therefore 4T.

questions.question: Concrete samples with and without glue capsules are stressed up to fracture. Explain how adding the glue capsules changes the properties of the concrete, using the stress-strain graphs.
questions.answer: The capsules leave the initial stiffness unchanged, but concrete B stands a much higher stress and strain before fracture, becomes stiffer and absorbs much more energy, so it is tougher
steps: At low stress and strain the two graphs coincide, so the gradient (Young modulus) at the start is the same: the capsules do not change the initial stiffness.
Sample A (plain concrete) fractures early, at low stress and strain, so the graph stops there.
Sample B carries on and its gradient increases: it becomes stiffer (larger stress for a given extra strain), because glue released from broken capsules fills the cracks and stops them spreading.
B reaches a maximum stress about 4 times that at which A fractures, so it can withstand a much greater force before breaking.
B also fractures at nearly twice the strain, so it can be deformed more before it breaks.
The area under the graph for B is much larger than for A, so B absorbs much more energy per unit volume before fracture: it is tougher.

questions.question: A wire of length x and diameter d extends by x under a tensile force. A second wire of the same material extends by 2x under the same force. Which row of the table could give its length and diameter? The table is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: A: length 0.5x, diameter 0.5d
steps: Extension = F L / (A E), so for the same force and material extension is proportional to L / d^2.
The first wire has extension proportional to x / d^2; the second needs twice this, so L / d^2 must double.
Row A: 0.5x / (0.5d)^2 = 2 x / d^2, which is double, so it is correct. Row B gives 1/8, row C gives 8 and row D gives 0.5 times the first wire.

questions.question: Temperature and tension affect the sag of a power cable. Suggest one further factor that may increase the sag.
questions.answer: The mass or weight of the cable per unit length (for example extra load from ice or wind), or a longer span between pylons.
steps: Sag depends on how much load the cable carries between its supports.
A heavier cable (greater mass per unit length) or extra load such as ice or wind increases the weight it must support.
The extra weight makes the cable hang lower, so the sag increases.

questions.question: A cable of mass M is at an angle theta to the horizontal at its supports. Explain why the tension in the cable decreases as the sag increases.
questions.answer: The vertical components of tension at the two supports must support the cable's weight, so 2T sin theta = Mg. As sag increases, theta increases, so T = Mg / (2 sin theta) decreases.
steps: The weight Mg of the cable is balanced by the vertical components of tension at the two supports: 2T sin theta = Mg.
The weight is fixed, so the total vertical component is fixed.
As the sag increases the cable is steeper at the supports, so theta increases.
Since sin theta increases, T = Mg / (2 sin theta) decreases.

questions.question: Using the stress-strain graph for steel in the ACSR cable, show that the Young modulus of steel is about 2 x 10^11 Pa. The graph is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: Young modulus of steel = gradient of the straight part = about 1.8 x 10^11 Pa, which is about 2 x 10^11 Pa
steps: The Young modulus is stress / strain, which is the gradient of the initial straight part of the steel line.
On the steel line, a stress of 100 MPa is reached at a strain of about 5.5 x 10^-4.
This is about 2 x 10^11 Pa to 1 significant figure.

questions.question: Pylons are 270 m apart. The cross-sectional area of one steel strand is 2.3 x 10^-6 m^2 and the tension per metre for steel is 0.62 N m^-1. Show that the stress in a steel strand is about 70 MPa.
questions.answer: Stress = 7.3 x 10^7 Pa, about 70 MPa
steps: Tension in the steel strand over the 270 m span = 0.62 x 270 = 167 N.
Stress = force / area = 167 / (2.3 x 10^-6) = 7.3 x 10^7 Pa.
This is about 70 MPa.

questions.question: Explain why ACSR cables have a steel core surrounded by aluminium strands. The extension of one aluminium strand due to the tension is 0.95 m. Include a calculation.
questions.answer: Steel has a much larger Young modulus, so it stretches far less (about 0.1 m versus 0.95 m for aluminium) and carries most of the tension; aluminium is light and a good conductor, so it carries the current.
steps: Steel's Young modulus is about 2 x 10^11 Pa, much higher than aluminium's.
Steel strand extension = strain x length = (stress / E) x L = (7.3 x 10^7 / 2 x 10^11) x 270 = 0.098 m.
The aluminium strand extends by 0.95 m, about ten times as much as the steel strand.
So the steel core limits the stretch and sag of the cable and carries most of the tension.
The aluminium strands are light and good conductors, so they carry the electrical current.

questions.question: A wire of material with a large Young modulus is tested. Which statement best describes the material: A large force per area to break it, B large mass per unit volume, C large ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain, or D returns to original length after a large stress?
questions.answer: C, the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain is large.
steps: Young modulus E = tensile stress / tensile strain.
A large value of E means a large stress is needed for a given strain, i.e. the material is stiff.
Option C describes exactly this ratio, so C is correct.

questions.question: The Young modulus of concrete increases as it dries. Using the stress-strain graphs for 2-day and 28-day samples, show that the Young modulus after drying is at least 1.3 times greater.
questions.answer: E(28 days) / E(2 days) = about 1.3 to 1.4, so the Young modulus is at least 1.3 times greater
steps: The Young modulus is the gradient of the initial straight part of each graph.
28-day sample: at strain 0.0010 the stress is about 44 MPa, so E = 44 x 10^6 / 0.0010 = 4.4 x 10^10 Pa.
2-day sample: at strain 0.0010 the stress is about 33 MPa, so E = 33 x 10^6 / 0.0010 = 3.3 x 10^10 Pa.
Ratio = 4.4 x 10^10 / 3.3 x 10^10 = 1.3 (1.33), so the Young modulus is at least 1.3 times greater.

questions.question: The 2-day sample absorbs 0.35 MJ m^-3 before fracture, and the 28-day sample absorbs less. Determine the percentage reduction in energy absorbed, given that the energy per unit volume is the area under the stress-strain graph.
questions.answer: The energy absorbed falls by about 11% (accept about 8% to 15%)
steps: Energy per unit volume is the area under the stress-strain graph. One large square is 0.001 x 20 MPa = 2.0 x 10^4 J m^-3 = 0.02 MJ m^-3.
The area under the 28-day graph up to fracture (strain 0.0040) is about 15.5 large squares = 0.31 MJ m^-3.
The 2-day sample absorbs 0.35 MJ m^-3 and the volumes are the same, so the fall is 0.35 - 0.31 = 0.04 MJ m^-3.
Percentage reduction = 0.04 / 0.35 x 100 = 11%.

questions.question: Manufacturers recommend leaving concrete blocks to dry for at least 28 days before use. Discuss why.
questions.answer: Concrete gains its full stiffness and strength as it cures and dries over about 28 days; wet concrete is weaker and less stiff, so it would not carry loads reliably.
steps: Concrete hardens (cures) as the cement reacts and the water content falls, so its strength and stiffness increase over time.
After 28 days the concrete has reached a stable, designed strength and Young modulus.
Concrete that is still wet has a lower Young modulus and strength, so it deforms more under load.
Using it early could give unpredictable or reduced strength, so a 28-day cure ensures reliable performance.

questions.question: Using the stress-strain graph for concrete (positive strain for compression, negative for tension), explain how it shows concrete is more suitable under compression than tension.
questions.answer: Concrete withstands a much greater stress (about 41 MPa) and strain in compression than in tension (about 10 MPa), so it is more suitable under compression
steps: Positive strain is compression: the stress rises to a maximum of about 41 MPa at a strain of about 0.3% before the concrete fractures.
Negative strain is tension: the stress reaches only about 10 MPa (in magnitude) at a strain of about -0.05%, and then fractures.
So concrete can take about 4 times the stress, and a larger strain, before breaking in compression than in tension, so it is better used in compression.

questions.question: A steel rod of diameter 45 mm is used. Using the steel stress-strain graph, calculate the maximum force before the rod fractures.
questions.answer: Maximum force = 8.1 x 10^5 N
steps: The greatest stress the steel withstands is the peak of the graph, about 5.1 x 10^8 Pa.
Cross-sectional area A = pi r^2 = pi x (22.5 x 10^-3)^2 = 1.59 x 10^-3 m^2.
Force = stress x area = 5.1 x 10^8 x 1.59 x 10^-3 = 8.1 x 10^5 N (using the slightly lower tension peak of about 4.9 x 10^8 Pa would give about 7.8 x 10^5 N).

questions.question: Steel rods are stretched while concrete is poured around them, then the force is removed so the concrete is placed in compression. Explain how this increases the maximum tensile force the concrete can withstand before fracture.
questions.answer: The steel pulls the concrete into compression; an external tensile force must first remove this compression before the concrete is put into tension, so a larger external force is needed to fracture it.
steps: The steel rods are stretched by the external force while the concrete sets around them.
When the external force is removed, the steel tries to contract and compresses the concrete.
Concrete is much stronger in compression than in tension, so this pre-compression is useful.
A larger external tensile force must first cancel this compression before the concrete is in net tension.
So the concrete can withstand a greater tensile force before it fractures.

questions.question: Explain why the external tensile force in the steel rods must not take the steel beyond its elastic limit.
questions.answer: If the steel went beyond its elastic limit it would stay permanently stretched, so it could not return to its original length to compress the concrete.
steps: Within the elastic limit, the steel returns to its original length when the external force is removed.
This recovery is what compresses the concrete.
Beyond the elastic limit the steel deforms plastically and stays longer than its original length.
The steel would then not exert the required compression on the concrete.

questions.question: State what is meant by elastic deformation.
questions.answer: Deformation that is fully reversed: the object returns to its original length and shape when the deforming force is removed.
steps: Elastic deformation is temporary.
When the deforming force is removed the object returns to its original length and shape.
No permanent change occurs.

questions.question: Using the compressive stress-strain graph for the metal, show that its Young modulus is about 2 x 10^11 Pa. The graph is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: Young modulus = gradient of the line = 2.1 x 10^11 Pa, which is about 2 x 10^11 Pa
steps: The Young modulus is stress / strain, which is the gradient of the straight line through the origin.
Using a large triangle, the line gives a stress of 4.2 x 10^8 Pa at a strain of 2.0 x 10^-3.

questions.topic: Suitability of Metal for a Part
questions.question: The part must not compress more than 0.60 mm under a force of 9.5 x 10^5 N. It has length 0.84 m and cross-sectional area 4.8 x 10^-3 m^2. The metal's Young modulus is about 2 x 10^11 Pa. Deduce whether the metal is suitable.
questions.answer: Not suitable: with E = 2 x 10^11 Pa the part would compress by about 0.83 mm, more than the 0.60 mm limit (a modulus of at least 2.8 x 10^11 Pa is needed).
steps: Compression = stress x L / E, so with E = 2 x 10^11 Pa the compression = 1.98 x 10^8 x 0.84 / (2 x 10^11) = 8.3 x 10^-4 m.
8.3 x 10^-4 m = 0.83 mm, which is more than the allowed 0.60 mm.
Required E = stress / max strain = 1.98 x 10^8 / (0.60 x 10^-3 / 0.84) = 2.8 x 10^11 Pa, so the metal is not suitable.

questions.question: A climber falls with fall factor 0.80 on a 15.0 m rope with maximum strain 9.0%, and mass 71 kg. Show that the maximum force on the climber due to the rope is about 10 kN, assuming extension is proportional to tension.
questions.answer: Maximum force = 1.4 x 10^4 N, which is about 1 x 10^4 N (10 kN) to 1 significant figure
steps: Fall factor = height fallen before the rope stretches / total unstretched length, so the height fallen = 0.80 x 15.0 = 12.0 m.
Maximum extension of the rope = 9.0% of 15.0 m = 1.35 m.
The climber loses gravitational potential energy over the whole distance 12.0 + 1.35 m: E = m g h = 71 x 9.81 x 13.35 = 9.3 x 10^3 J.
This is all stored as elastic strain energy. As extension is proportional to tension, E = (1/2) F x, so F = 2E / x = 2 x 9.3 x 10^3 / 1.35 = 1.4 x 10^4 N.
1.4 x 10^4 N is about 1 x 10^4 N = 10 kN to 1 significant figure.

questions.question: A new climber suggests using a longer rope between the loop and the climber, as it would absorb more energy after a fall. Comment on this suggestion.
questions.answer: The suggestion is not a good one: a longer rope allows a longer fall, so more energy must be absorbed, and it does not reduce the peak force for the same fall factor.
steps: The energy the rope must absorb equals the climber's loss of gravitational potential energy during the fall.
A longer rope increases the distance the climber falls before the rope is taut, so more energy must be absorbed.
The peak force depends on the fall factor (fall distance / rope length) and strain, not on the rope length alone.
So a longer rope does not make the rope safer for the same fall factor, and it increases the fall distance.

questions.question: Manufacturers recommend replacing climbing ropes every 5 years. Force-extension graphs for a 1 m length of new rope and of rope after 5 years are shown. Comment on the recommendation, including calculations.
questions.answer: The recommendation is sensible: after 5 years the rope breaks at about 13 kN instead of 18 kN, stretches about twice as far under the same force, and absorbs less energy before breaking
steps: Breaking force: the new rope breaks at about 18 x 10^3 N (extension 0.13 m); the 5-year-old rope breaks at only about 13 x 10^3 N (extension 0.18 m), about 30% lower.
Stiffness: at a force of 5000 N the new rope extends about 0.07 m, but the old rope extends about 0.13 m, so the old rope is much less stiff.
Energy absorbed to break 1 m (area under each graph): new rope about 790 J, old rope about 660 J, about 16% less.
A hard fall can produce a force of the order of 14 kN (part (a)), which is more than the old rope can stand (13 kN) but less than the new rope (18 kN), so the aged rope could break.
The aged rope also stretches more, so a falling climber would travel further before being stopped.
So the manufacturers are right: the rope weakens with age, and replacing it after 5 years keeps a safe margin.

questions.question: State what is meant by the yield point of a material.
questions.answer: The stress at which the material begins to deform plastically, so it does not return to its original length when the stress is removed.
steps: The yield point is the point at which the material starts to deform permanently.
Beyond it, the extension is no longer fully recovered when the stress is removed.

questions.question: Explain why the forces on the actor make him accelerate upwards when he is lifted by the cable and harness.
questions.answer: The tension in the cable is greater than the actor's weight, so the resultant force is upwards and he accelerates upwards.
steps: The forces on the actor are the upward tension in the cable and his weight acting downwards.
Tension is greater than weight, so the resultant force is upwards.
By Newton's second law, a resultant upward force gives an upward acceleration.

questions.question: The actor has mass 77 kg and is lifted vertically with acceleration 2.1 m s^-2. Show that the tension in the cable is about 920 N.
questions.answer: T = m(g + a) = 917 N, about 920 N
steps: Newton's second law upwards: T - mg = ma.
T = 77 x 11.91 = 917 N, which is about 920 N.

questions.question: The stress in the cable must be less than 15% of its yield point stress of 2.5 x 10^8 Pa. The cable diameter is 7.6 x 10^-3 m and the tension is about 917 N. Deduce whether it is safe to lift the actor with acceleration 2.1 m s^-2.
questions.answer: Yes, it is safe: the stress is about 2.0 x 10^7 Pa, below the limit of 3.75 x 10^7 Pa (15% of the yield stress).
steps: Cross-sectional area A = pi (d/2)^2 = pi x (3.8 x 10^-3)^2 = 4.54 x 10^-5 m^2.
2.0 x 10^7 Pa is less than 3.75 x 10^7 Pa, so the lift is safe.

questions.question: The cable is replaced by one of the same length and the same breaking stress, but made of a material with a lower Young modulus and with a greater diameter. Explain how the work done to break the new cable differs from that for the original cable, assuming Hooke's law applies up to breaking.
questions.answer: The new cable needs more work to break: the energy stored per unit volume at breaking (sigma^2 / 2E) is larger because E is lower, and the greater cross-sectional area gives a larger volume.
steps: Work done to break = elastic strain energy stored = (1/2) x stress x strain x volume = sigma^2 V / (2E).
The breaking stress sigma is the same for both cables.
Lower Young modulus E gives a larger energy per unit volume, sigma^2 / (2E).
Greater diameter gives a greater cross-sectional area, so the volume V = A x L is larger for the same length.
Both effects increase the energy, so more work is done to break the new cable.

questions.question: State what is meant by the limit of proportionality.
questions.answer: The maximum stress (or force) up to which extension is directly proportional to the applied force (Hooke's law is obeyed).
steps: Up to the limit of proportionality, extension is directly proportional to force.
Beyond it, the graph of force against extension is no longer a straight line through the origin.

questions.question: Determine the gradient of the student's weight against extension graph for the stainless steel wire.
questions.answer: Gradient = 1.9 x 10^4 N m^-1 (about 18.5 N per 10^-3 m)
steps: Draw a large triangle on the best-fit line, which passes through the origin.
At an extension of 2.0 x 10^-3 m the line gives a weight of about 37 N.

questions.question: Using the gradient from part (b)(i), determine the Young modulus of stainless steel for a wire of unstretched length 2.6 m and diameter 5.6 x 10^-4 m.
questions.answer: Young modulus = 2.0 x 10^11 Pa
steps: Gradient of the weight-extension graph = F / x = 1.85 x 10^4 N m^-1.
Young modulus E = (F / A) / (x / L) = gradient x L / A.

questions.question: The breaking stress of the stainless steel wire (diameter 5.6 x 10^-4 m) is 480 MPa. Deduce whether it is safe to increase the weight to 100.0 N.
questions.answer: Yes, it is safe from breaking: the stress is about 406 MPa, below the breaking stress of 480 MPa.
steps: Cross-sectional area A = pi (d/2)^2 = pi x (2.8 x 10^-4)^2 = 2.46 x 10^-7 m^2.
406 MPa is less than the breaking stress of 480 MPa, so the wire will not break.

questions.question: State two reasons why the weight of the steel object and the electromagnet force on it are not a Newton third law pair.
questions.answer: Both forces act on the same object, whereas a Newton third law pair acts on two different objects; and the weight and magnetic force are not reactions of each other (the weight's pair is the pull of the object on the Earth).
steps: A Newton third law pair acts on two different bodies.
Both the weight and the electromagnet force act on the same steel object.
The partner of the weight is the object's gravitational pull on the Earth, not the magnetic force.
So the two forces are not a third law pair.

questions.question: The steel cable has cross-sectional area 5.1 x 10^-4 m^2, unstretched length 3.8 m and stiffness 2.8 x 10^7 N m^-1. When the object is suspended the strain is 3.0 x 10^-4. Calculate the Young modulus of the steel.
questions.answer: Young modulus = 2.1 x 10^11 Pa
steps: Stiffness k = EA / L, so E = k L / A.
E = 2.09 x 10^11 Pa, which is about 2.1 x 10^11 Pa.

questions.topic: Elastic Strain Energy and Energy Transfer
questions.question: The electromagnet is switched off and the steel object falls. A student says the elastic strain energy in the cable is transferred to the gravitational potential energy of the electromagnet. Discuss this statement, adding to the force-extension graph.
questions.answer: Not correct as stated: only part of the elastic energy released becomes gravitational potential energy; the rest becomes kinetic energy of the electromagnet, which then oscillates and is dissipated as heat
steps: Before the object falls the cable supports the total weight W_total, and the extension is x2, with elastic energy equal to the area under the graph up to x2.
On the graph draw a horizontal line at the weight of the electromagnet alone, W_m. It meets the graph at the new equilibrium extension x1, less than x2.
The decrease in elastic energy is the area under the graph between x1 and x2, a trapezoid equal to (1/2)(W_m + W_total)(x2 - x1).
The gain in gravitational potential energy of the electromagnet is W_m (x2 - x1), the rectangle under the W_m line, which is smaller than the trapezoid.

The remaining energy (the triangle above the rectangle) becomes kinetic energy of the electromagnet, which oscillates, and is dissipated as thermal energy, so the student's statement is not correct in general (all of it becomes GPE only at the very top of the first oscillation if there are no losses).

questions.question: Explain why the stiffness of a rope becomes smaller the greater its length.
questions.answer: For a rope of given material and cross-section, stiffness k = EA / L, so a longer rope has a smaller stiffness and stretches more for the same force.
steps: For the same material and cross-sectional area, the stiffness is k = EA / L.
Increasing the length L decreases k.
So a longer rope extends more under the same force, i.e. it is less stiff.

questions.question: The nylon rope has Young modulus 2.70 GPa, cross-sectional area 3.00 x 10^-4 m^2 and length 6.00 m. Show that its stiffness is about 1.4 x 10^5 N m^-1.
steps: Stiffness k = EA / L.
k = 1.35 x 10^5 N m^-1, which is about 1.4 x 10^5 N m^-1.

questions.question: The pulley system (one fixed and one movable pulley) lifts a 5.00 kN load at a steady rate. Using the rope stiffness of 1.35 x 10^5 N m^-1, determine the extension of the rope during the lift.
questions.answer: Extension = 0.0185 m, about 0.019 m (1.9 cm)
steps: The movable pulley is supported by two rope strands, so each strand carries half the load: T = 5000 / 2 = 2500 N.
At a steady rate the forces balance, so the rope tension is 2500 N.

questions.question: Calculate the work done in stretching the nylon rope during the lift.
questions.answer: Work done = 23 J
steps: Work done = (1/2) x tension x extension, since the force rises linearly from zero.

questions.question: Assess whether the stretching of the rope has a significant effect on the efficiency of the pulley system.
questions.answer: No, not significant: the energy stored in stretching the rope (about 23 J) is only about 0.3% of the useful work of lifting the load through 1.50 m (7500 J).
steps: Useful work done in lifting the load = 5000 x 1.50 = 7500 J.
Energy stored in stretching the rope = 23 J.
23 / 7500 = 0.3%, which is very small, so the effect on efficiency is negligible.

questions.topic: Work Done in Stretching a Wire
questions.question: A stress is applied across the ends of a wire of cross-sectional area A. Work W is done to extend the wire by x. Which expression could be used to determine W? The options are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: C: W = (1/2) x sigma x A x delta x
steps: Force F = stress x area = sigma A.
For a wire obeying Hooke's law, work done = area under the force-extension graph = (1/2) F delta x.
So W = (1/2) x sigma x A x delta x, which is option C.

questions.question: A stress-strain graph up to breaking point is drawn for four wire samples A to D. Which sample has both a low elastic limit and a large region of plastic deformation? The graph and options are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: C
steps: A low elastic limit means the curve levels off at a low stress, so the candidates are C and D (A and B have much higher stress).
A large region of plastic deformation means a long flat part of the graph before breaking, i.e. a large strain range at nearly constant stress.
C has the longer plastic region (it extends to a larger strain than D), so C is correct.

questions.question: An object of mass m rests on a compressed spring, which returns to its original length, and the object has speed v at that point. Which equation describes the energy transfer? The options are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: B: (1/2) F delta x = (1/2) m v^2 + m g delta x
steps: The force rises from zero to F as the spring is compressed by delta x, so the energy stored is (1/2) F delta x.
As the spring returns to its original length the object rises by delta x, so it gains gravitational potential energy m g delta x.
The rest of the energy is kinetic: (1/2) F delta x = (1/2) m v^2 + m g delta x, which is option B.

questions.question: Two springs S1 and S2 hang with masses attached. S1 extends by x and stores elastic strain energy E. Which expression gives the strain energy in S2? The extension of S2 and the options are shown in the figure below.
steps: Elastic energy = (1/2) F x, where F is the weight hanging on the spring.
S1: force mg and extension x, so E = (1/2) m g x.
S2: force 2mg and extension x/3, so energy = (1/2)(2mg)(x/3) = (2/3)(1/2) m g x = 2E / 3, option C.

questions.topic: Bungee Jump Energy and Work Done
questions.question: Explain, in terms of work done, how the kinetic energy of a bungee jumper changes during three stages: free fall until the cord starts to stretch; stretching until the acceleration is zero; and stretching until momentarily at rest.
questions.answer: KE increases in stage 1 and in the early part of stage 2 (weight does more positive work than the cord); KE is maximum when acceleration is zero; in stage 3 the cord does more negative work than the weight, so KE falls to zero.
steps: Stage 1: only the weight does work on the jumper; the work done is positive, so KE increases.
Stage 2: the cord exerts an upward force that does negative work, but while the cord force is less than the weight, the weight still does more positive work and KE increases.
At the end of stage 2 the cord force equals the weight, so the resultant force and acceleration are zero and KE is at its maximum.
Beyond that point the cord force exceeds the weight, so the net work done is negative and KE decreases.
Stage 3: the cord does more negative work than the weight does positive work, so KE falls steadily to zero at the momentary rest.

questions.question: A spring stretched by force F stores energy E. Three identical springs in parallel are stretched by a force 2F. Which expression gives the total elastic energy? The options are shown in the figure below.
steps: For one spring, E = (1/2) F x = F^2 / (2k), so energy is proportional to (force)^2.
The three identical springs share 2F equally, so each carries 2F / 3.
Energy in each = (2/3)^2 E = 4E / 9, and for three springs the total is 3 x 4E / 9 = 4E / 3.

questions.question: A rubber band is stretched and returned to its original length. Using the force-extension graph with areas P, Q and R, which expression gives the work done in stretching it to maximum extension? The graph is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: B: Q + R
steps: The work done in stretching is the area under the upper (loading) curve, from zero to maximum extension.
The area under the lower (unloading) curve is R, and the area between the two curves is Q.
So the area under the loading curve is Q + R. Area P lies above the curve and is not part of the work done.

questions.question: Using a force-extension graph for a spring, which expression gives the work done in joules to extend the spring by 0.30 m from its original length? The graph and options are shown in the figure below.
steps: The graph is a straight line through the origin, so the work done is the area of a triangle = (1/2) x force x extension.
At an extension of 0.30 m the graph reads a force of about 2.5 N.
Work = 0.5 x 0.30 x 2.5 J, which is option B.

questions.topic: Springs in Series and Parallel Energy
questions.question: Arrangements P and Q of identical springs are subject to the same tensile force F, and one spring alone stores energy E. Which row of the table gives the total strain energy in each arrangement? The diagram and table are shown in the figure below.
steps: P: two identical springs in series each carry the full force F, so each stores E and the total is 2E.
Q: the two springs are in parallel, so the force F is shared and each carries F/2.
Energy is proportional to force squared, so each stores E/4 and the total is E/2, which gives row D.

questions.question: A steel wire fixed at one end has an increasing force applied to the other end. Which row of the table identifies points P, Q and R on the force-extension graph? The graph and table are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: C: P is the yield point, Q the elastic limit and R the limit of proportionality
steps: Moving along the graph from the origin, the first point to be reached is the end of the straight line, R, the limit of proportionality.
Q is a little further along, just beyond R: the elastic limit.
P is the peak just before the dip in the curve where the wire starts to stretch with little extra force: the yield point.

questions.question: A glider is pulled back on an elastic cord that obeys Hooke's law, then released. Explain why conservation of energy predicts a straight-line graph through the origin of maximum velocity against extension.
questions.answer: Elastic energy 1/2 k x^2 is all converted to kinetic energy 1/2 m v^2, so v = x sqrt(k/m), a straight line through the origin.
steps: Energy stored in the cord (Hooke's law region) = (1/2) k x^2.
At maximum speed, all this elastic energy is converted to kinetic energy of the glider = (1/2) m v^2 (no losses).
So (1/2) m v^2 = (1/2) k x^2, giving v = x sqrt(k / m).
For constant k and m, v is proportional to x, so the graph is a straight line through the origin.

questions.question: Using the graph of maximum velocity against extension for the elastic cord, and a glider mass of 300 g, determine the stiffness k of the cord.
steps: Energy conservation: (1/2) k (delta x)^2 = (1/2) m v^2, so v = delta x sqrt(k / m) and the gradient of the graph = sqrt(k / m).
Gradient of the best-fit line = (4.4 - 1.8) / (0.50 - 0.20) = 8.7 s^-1.
k = m x gradient^2 = 0.300 x 8.7^2 = 23 N m^-1.

questions.question: When the glider was pulled more than 0.5 m to the right, the graph began to curve. Explain why the shape of the graph changed.
questions.answer: Beyond about 0.5 m the cord stretches past its limit of proportionality, so Hooke's law no longer applies and the force, and hence the energy stored, is no longer proportional to the extension.
steps: Up to 0.5 m the cord obeys Hooke's law, so the force and energy are proportional to extension (energy proportional to x squared).
Beyond 0.5 m the cord passes its limit of proportionality.
The stiffness is no longer constant, so the energy stored and velocity no longer follow the straight-line relation.

questions.question: A force F compresses a spring by x. A second spring with double the stiffness is compressed by the same distance x. Which expression gives the force on the second spring? The options are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: B: 2F
steps: Hooke's law: F = k x, so for the same compression the force is proportional to the stiffness.
Doubling the stiffness at the same compression doubles the force: 2F.

questions.question: Several graphs are drawn and the area under each represents a physical quantity. For which graph is the area not equal to work done? The graphs are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: D: stress against strain
steps: Force against displacement: area = force x distance = work done.
Force against extension: area = work done in stretching.
Power against time: area = power x time = energy transferred = work done.
Stress against strain: area = (force / area) x (extension / length) = energy per unit volume, not work done. So D is the exception.

questions.question: A 12 g ball is launched at 8.0 cm s^-1 from a spring. Show that its kinetic energy is about 4 x 10^-5 J.
questions.answer: Ek = 3.8 x 10^-5 J, about 4 x 10^-5 J
steps: Convert: m = 0.012 kg and v = 0.080 m s^-1.

questions.question: The spring is compressed by 5.0 cm and then released, launching the ball. Using the kinetic energy from part (a), determine the force on the ball when the spring is released.
questions.answer: Average force over the 5.0 cm launch = 7.7 x 10^-4 N (the peak force is twice this).
steps: Work done by the spring = kinetic energy gained = 3.84 x 10^-5 J.
Work done = F d, so the average force F = 3.84 x 10^-5 / 0.050 m.
F = 7.7 x 10^-4 N, the average force during the launch.

questions.question: Using the kinetic energy of the ball and the compression of 5.0 cm, determine the stiffness of the spring.
questions.answer: Stiffness = 0.031 N m^-1
steps: All the stored elastic potential energy becomes kinetic energy: (1/2) k x^2 = 3.84 x 10^-5 J.

questions.question: The spring returns to its original length L. Sketch a graph of the ball's velocity against the length of the spring.
questions.answer: A curve starting at zero velocity at a length below L (the compressed length), rising with decreasing gradient to a maximum velocity at L, where the gradient is zero
steps: The spring starts compressed (length less than L, to the left of L on the axis) with the ball at rest, so the curve starts on the length axis at v = 0.
As the spring extends, the ball speeds up, but the spring force falls, so the acceleration decreases and the curve becomes less steep.
At the original length L the spring force is zero (no acceleration), so the velocity is at its maximum and the curve is horizontal there.
The shape is a quarter of an ellipse from (compressed length, 0) to (L, v_max), because (1/2) m v^2 = (1/2) k (x0^2 - x^2).

questions.topic: Limit of Proportionality on Loading Graph
questions.question: A student loads a spring and plots position against load for loading and unloading. State the significance of point K on the graph.
questions.answer: Point K is the limit of proportionality: beyond K the force is no longer proportional to the extension
steps: Up to K the loading graph is a straight line through the origin, so force is proportional to extension (Hooke's law obeyed).
At K the line starts to curve, so K is the limit of proportionality.

questions.question: The load is increased until the spring exceeds its elastic limit at point L. Explain the significance of point L.
questions.answer: Point L is the elastic limit: beyond it the spring no longer returns to its original length when the load is removed, because it has been permanently deformed.
steps: Up to the elastic limit the spring returns to its original length when unloaded.
At point L the spring has exceeded its elastic limit.
Beyond L it is permanently deformed and does not fully recover its original length.

questions.question: The unloading graph has a different gradient from the loading graph. Suggest why.
questions.answer: The spring was stretched beyond its elastic limit and is permanently deformed, so its behaviour on unloading differs from that on loading.
steps: The spring was loaded beyond its elastic limit at point L.
This causes permanent (plastic) deformation of the spring.
So the unloading path does not follow the loading path, giving a different gradient.

questions.question: A second student forgets to subtract the original length of the spring from the measurements. Sketch the shape of the graph he would obtain for loading.
questions.answer: A straight line with the same gradient as before, but not through the origin: it starts on the extension axis at a positive value equal to the original length, then curves like the first graph beyond the limit of proportionality
steps: He plots the length (original length + extension) instead of the extension.
With no load the plotted value is the original length, so the graph starts on the horizontal axis at a positive value, not at the origin.
Every point is shifted to the right by the same amount, so the straight part is parallel to the correct graph (same gradient).

questions.question: Two identical springs are connected in series. Explain why the spring constant for this arrangement is half that of one spring.
questions.answer: In series each spring carries the same force F and the extensions add, so total extension = 2F/k and effective stiffness = F / (2F/k) = k/2.
steps: In series, the same force F acts through each spring.
Each spring extends by x = F / k, so the total extension is 2F / k.
The effective stiffness is k_eff = F / (total extension) = F / (2F / k).
So k_eff = k / 2: the arrangement is half as stiff as one spring.

questions.question: A copper rod is put under tensile stress and the stress is plotted against strain. What does point X represent? Options: A fracture point, B limit of proportionality, C maximum stress, D yield point. The graph is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: D: the yield point of copper
steps: X is the peak of the curve after the initial steep rise, followed by a drop in stress.
After this point the rod stretches a lot with little or no increase in stress, which is the yield point.
It is not the fracture point or the maximum stress (the curve rises higher later), so D is correct.

questions.question: Which statement could be used to describe the elastic limit of a material? A the stress above which it will not obey Hooke's law, B the stress above which it is deformed when the stress is removed, C the stress at which a sudden increase in extension occurs, D the stress at which it breaks.
questions.answer: B, the stress above which the material is deformed when the stress is removed.
steps: The elastic limit is the stress beyond which deformation becomes permanent.
Option B describes this: the material remains deformed after the stress is removed.
Option A describes the limit of proportionality, not the elastic limit.

questions.question: State how the graph of extension against force for the rubber band shows that it deformed elastically.
questions.answer: The extension returns to zero when the force is reduced to zero (the decreasing-force curve ends at the origin), so the band returns to its original length
steps: Elastic deformation means the object returns to its original length when the force is removed.
On the graph, when the force falls back to zero the extension is also back to zero.

questions.topic: Energy Lost as Heat in Rubber
questions.question: The work done on the rubber band while the force increases is greater than the work done by the band as the force decreases, because heating occurred. Determine the energy that caused heating.
questions.answer: Energy that caused heating = 0.050 J (about 5 x 10^-2 J)
steps: Work done on the band as force increases = area under the increasing-force curve, which is about 10.7 N cm.
Work done by the band as force decreases = area under the decreasing-force curve, about 5.7 N cm.
The energy that caused heating is the difference, which is the area between the curves = about 5.0 N cm.
1 N cm = 0.01 J, so the energy = 5.0 x 0.01 = 0.050 J (accept about 0.045 to 0.055 J).

questions.topic: Comparing Wires from Stress Strain Graphs
questions.question: Two wires P and Q of different metals are stretched to breaking, and their stress-strain graphs are shown. Which statement is correct: A P has greater breaking stress, B P has greater breaking strain, C P has greater yield stress, D P has lower Young modulus? The graph is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: C: P has a greater yield stress than Q
steps: P has the steeper initial line, so it has the greater Young modulus (D is false).
P's first peak (the yield stress) is higher than Q's, so C is true.
Q ends at a higher stress and a larger strain than P, so P has a lower breaking stress (A false) and a lower breaking strain (B false).

questions.question: Which of these is an SI unit for stress? A kg m^-2, B m^2 kg^-2, C m^2 N^-1, D N m^-2.
questions.answer: D, N m^-2 (equivalent to the pascal).
steps: Stress = force / area, so its unit is N / m^2 = N m^-2.
N m^-2 is the pascal, the SI unit of stress.
The other options do not give force per unit area.

questions.question: A wire broke at a small extension. A second wire of the same material had a larger extension before breaking. Which of these produced this result: A greater diameter, B longer length, C smaller diameter, D shorter length?
questions.answer: B, the second wire had a longer length.
steps: Same material means the same breaking strain.
Extension at breaking = breaking strain x original length.
A larger extension before breaking therefore needs a longer original length: option B.

questions.question: Which description applies to a thin metal wire at its elastic limit: A elastically deformed, B plastically deformed, C maximum extension, D snaps?
questions.answer: A, the wire is still elastically deformed.
steps: At the elastic limit the wire is at the boundary of elastic behaviour.
Up to and including this point, deformation is still fully recoverable.
Plastic deformation only begins beyond the elastic limit, and the wire does not snap at this point.

questions.question: A spring is stretched by a force of 3.0 N and stores 0.04 J of elastic strain energy. Which expression gives the extension in m? The options are shown in the figure below.
steps: Elastic strain energy E = (1/2) F x.
So the extension x = 2E / F = 2 x 0.04 / 3.0 = 0.027 m, which is option A.

questions.question: Which expression gives the work done in stretching a spring from its original length p to length q? The options are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: B: (q - p) x R / 2 (taking R as the final stretching force, which is not defined on this page)
steps: The extension is the new length minus the original length: q - p.
For a spring obeying Hooke's law the work done is the area of a triangle = (1/2) x force x extension.
With R the final force, work = (q - p) x R / 2, which is option B.

questions.topic: Force from Stress in Spider Silk
questions.question: A spider silk thread has stress 4.3 MPa and radius 1.9 x 10^-6 m. Calculate the force applied to the thread.
questions.answer: Force = 4.9 x 10^-5 N
steps: Cross-sectional area A = pi r^2 = pi x (1.9 x 10^-6)^2 = 1.13 x 10^-11 m^2.
Force = stress x area = 4.3 x 10^6 x 1.13 x 10^-11.
Force = 4.9 x 10^-5 N.

questions.question: A 25.0 m spider silk thread is stretched to its limit of proportionality where the stress is 300 MPa, with Young modulus 8.70 GPa. Determine the length of the thread at this point.
questions.answer: Length at limit of proportionality = 25.9 m
steps: Strain at limit = stress / E = (3.00 x 10^8) / (8.70 x 10^9) = 0.0345.
Extension = strain x original length = 0.0345 x 25.0 m = 0.862 m.

questions.question: Add a line to the sketch stress-strain graph for spider silk to show the stress-strain relationship for steel up to its limit of proportionality, using the table of properties.
questions.answer: Draw a much steeper straight line from the origin, ending at a slightly higher stress (350 MPa against 300 MPa) at a much smaller strain than the spider silk line
steps: Steel has Young modulus 200 GPa, about 23 times that of spider silk (8.70 GPa), so its line is 23 times as steep.
Strain at the limit of proportionality for steel = 350 x 10^6 / 200 x 10^9 = 1.75 x 10^-3, compared with 0.0345 for the silk, so about 1/20 as far along the strain axis.
Stress at the end of the steel line is 350 MPa, about 17% higher than the 300 MPa at the end of the silk line.

questions.question: Samples of steel and spider silk of identical shape, length and cross-sectional area are each stretched to their limit of proportionality. Explain which sample has the greater elastic strain energy. The table of properties is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: The spider silk stores the greater elastic strain energy (about 17 times more per unit volume)
steps: The samples have the same volume, so compare the energy per unit volume = (1/2) x stress x strain at the limit of proportionality (area under the graph).
The silk therefore stores about 17 times more energy, because it stretches to a much larger strain even though its stress limit is lower.

questions.question: A rope sample of original length 36.8 m increases in length to 38.1 m. Calculate the strain.
questions.answer: Strain = 0.0353
steps: Extension = 38.1 - 36.8 = 1.3 m.
Strain = extension / original length = 1.3 / 36.8.
Strain = 0.0353 (no units).

questions.question: The rope has diameter 220 mm. Using its stress-strain graph, determine the force applied when the strain is 0.025.
questions.answer: Force = 4.2 x 10^6 N
steps: From the graph, at a strain of 0.025 the stress is about 110 MPa (110 x 10^6 Pa).
Cross-sectional area A = pi r^2 = pi x (0.110)^2 = 3.80 x 10^-2 m^2 (diameter 220 mm, radius 0.110 m).
Force = stress x area = 110 x 10^6 x 3.80 x 10^-2 = 4.2 x 10^6 N.

questions.question: Explain how the area under the stress-strain graph and the volume of the sample can be used to determine the energy stored.
questions.answer: The area under the stress-strain graph gives the energy stored per unit volume; multiplying by the volume of the sample gives the total energy stored.
steps: Stress is force per area and strain is extension per length, so stress x strain has units of energy per unit volume.
The area under the stress-strain graph (up to the point considered) equals the energy stored per unit volume.
Multiplying this energy density by the volume of the sample gives the total energy stored.

questions.question: Which of the following gives the Young modulus of the material from its stress-strain graph? A the area between the line and the strain axis, B the gradient of the graph, C maximum stress x maximum strain, D maximum strain / maximum stress.
questions.answer: B, the gradient of the graph.
steps: Young modulus E = stress / strain.
On a stress-strain graph the gradient is stress divided by strain (in the linear region).
So the gradient of the graph gives the Young modulus: option B.

questions.question: A spring is stretched beyond its elastic limit and the force is then removed. Which description is correct? A extension always proportional to force, B plastic deformation until the elastic limit is reached, C only elastic deformation, D does not return to its original length.
questions.answer: D, the spring does not return to its original length.
steps: Beyond the elastic limit the spring is permanently (plastically) deformed.
So when the force is removed it does not return to its original length.
Option D is the only description consistent with this.

questions.topic: Elastic Strain Energy from Force-Compression Graph
questions.question: Determine the increase in elastic strain energy in a brick as the force increases from 85 N to 140 N, using the force-compression graph.
questions.answer: Increase in elastic strain energy = 4.3 x 10^-6 J
steps: The energy stored is the area under the force-compression graph, so the increase is the area between the two forces.
Reading the graph: 85 N corresponds to a compression of about 59 nm and 140 N to about 97 nm.

questions.question: The brick undergoes elastic deformation. State what is meant by elastic deformation.
questions.answer: The brick returns to its original shape and size when the deforming force is removed.
steps: Elastic deformation is temporary.
When the force is removed, the brick returns to its original shape and size.

questions.question: A force-extension graph for a sample of one violin string, and a table of stiffnesses for three other strings of the same original length, are given. Deduce which string was used to obtain the graph.
questions.answer: String Y: the graph gradient (stiffness) is about 2.7 x 10^3 N m^-1
steps: The graph is a straight line through the origin, so the stiffness k = force / extension = gradient.
Using a large triangle: force 80 N at an extension of 29.4 mm = 0.0294 m.
The strings have the same original length, so their stiffnesses can be compared directly: 2700 N m^-1 matches string Y (X is 1700 and Z is 6100).

questions.question: The fourth violin string has original length 0.750 m and radius 0.85 x 10^-3 m. A tension of 36 N lengthens it to 0.752 m. Determine the Young modulus of the string material.
questions.answer: Young modulus = 5.9 x 10^9 Pa
steps: Cross-sectional area A = pi r^2 = pi x (0.85 x 10^-3)^2 = 2.27 x 10^-6 m^2.
